extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians and advanced mathematics students (algebra, geometry, analysis, mechanics)
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of short 19th-century mathematical notes giving theorems, derivation rules, and constructive methods in algebra (transformations of equations), projective/curve geometry (involution relations), integral reduction, roof equilibrium (mechanics), and numerical synthesis (Horner).

rubrics_metrics.name: Locus degree when dividing intersections in given ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: If a straight line AP, drawn through a given point A, meets a curve of the mth degree in Q1,...,Qm and a curve of the nth degree in P1,...,Pn, and if P is taken so that the segments are divided in a given ratio, then the locus of P is a curve of degree m+n passing through the m·n points of intersection of the two given curves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special case noted: when two conics meet in six points, the constructed locus is a cubic passing through the six intersection points. In general the degree of the locus equals the sum of the degrees of the two given curves; the locus passes through all pairwise intersection points (real or imaginary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Involution from three conics through four common points (Sturm)
rubrics_metrics.description: If three conic sections (C), (C'), (C'') pass through the same four points and an arbitrary transversal from fixed A meets them in pairs P,P'; Q,Q'; R,R', then the six points P,P',Q,Q',R,R' on the transversal are in involution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as an extension/corollary of Pappus/Desargues and follows from the general theorem on transversals; it is due to Sturm. Use elimination/ratio relations among directed segments on the transversal to establish the involution.

rubrics_metrics.name: General involution relations for three curves
rubrics_metrics.description: For three curves of given degrees (e.g., third degree) each passing through the intersection points of the other two, the segments into which a transversal is cut satisfy a system of algebraic relations which may be described as involutions of 2n+2, 2n+2, or m+n+2 points (depending on degrees).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper gives explicit multiplicative relations among segment-products (analogies and eliminations) and notes that from the primary set of equations many other relations are obtainable by elimination or multiplication; these relations are called involutions of 2n+2, 2n+2, m+n+2 points as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express relations in symmetric functions and eliminate roots
rubrics_metrics.description: To construct transformations of algebraic equations, express relations among coefficients in symmetric functions of the roots and eliminate one root between the relations to obtain the resulting equation; identical resulting equations indicate interchangeable conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The method is presented as a general framework: given a relation among coefficients and a relation among roots, rewrite them in symmetric functions, eliminate a chosen root (e.g. v) to produce the transformed equation; interchangeable (identical) resulting equations show equivalence of conditions. This approach provides latitude in choosing auxiliary functions for transformations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetry preservation under derived symmetric functions
rubrics_metrics.description: If a symmetric function φ (of the roots) is symmetric, then the derived functions φ', φ'', ... obtained by the standard constructions are also symmetric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text outlines a combinatorial argument: grouping terms and comparing sums shows that derived functions inherit symmetry; use this to justify use of symmetric forms throughout transformation manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule to derive φ' from φ (multiplicative/division rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain φ' (a derived symmetric function) from φ, multiply by (n−1) and divide each term by the number of distinct roots which enter into that term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated as a concrete computational rule (see p.84 reference): 'multiply by n−1, and divide each term by the number of different roots which enter into that term.' The paper notes that neglecting the division/multiplicative adjustments led to prior errors and gives corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply correction multipliers when counting term-multiplicities
rubrics_metrics.description: When performing the derivation/multiplication operations on symmetric terms, include combinatorial multipliers corresponding to how many times a term is generated (counts of permutations) to avoid arithmetic errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author reports having to multiply certain terms by 2 or 3 in earlier lines to correct omissions. Practical guidance: track how many times a term appears under permutations and apply that factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of auxiliary decompositions to extend transformation methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine the decomposition of symmetric relations with existing transformation techniques (e.g., Jerrard's method) to extend applicability to lower-degree equations and to create admissibility tests for assumptions about root forms for higher degrees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author outlines how decomposing a condition into simpler homogeneous components can avoid causes of failure in classical methods and can be used to push transformations beyond previously known degree limits; details are given for specific decompositions (p.114–116 references).

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling assumptions for equilibrium of symmetrical roof
rubrics_metrics.description: For a roof of uniform beams symmetrical about a vertical axis: treat each uniform beam as its weight concentrated at its midpoint; vertical pressure from a beam is split equally between its two ends; the horizontal thrust H is constant throughout the roof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These modeling assumptions permit writing equilibrium equations at each joint (A, B, C, ...). Use standard statics: resolve pressures into components and apply Lami's theorem to relate magnitudes by sines of angles between directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Lami's theorem to relate pressures at joints
rubrics_metrics.description: At each joint where three forces are in equilibrium, each force is proportional to the sine of the angle between the other two (Lami's principle), enabling explicit trigonometric equilibrium equations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Lami's theorem at the ridge and at successive joints to produce equations linking H, beam-weight contributions, and angles; combine successive equations to eliminate H and derive relations (e.g., tan relations) determining beam inclinations and roof geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure to determine roof geometry from equilibrium equations
rubrics_metrics.description: From the derived trigonometric equilibrium relations (sums involving tan and sine/cosine of beam angles and proportional weights), eliminate variables to obtain polynomial equations (example: quartic) whose real positive roots give beam angles and hence roof height.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example provided: symmetric roof with given spans and beam lengths leads to two trigonometric equations which reduce to a fourth-degree equation; solve the polynomial to obtain angles and then compute heights and beam positions back-substituting into original relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction of integrals via finite differences and differentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Some complicated integrals can be reduced to simpler known integrals by taking successive finite differences with respect to a parameter and differentiating with respect to that parameter, then using algebraic identities to express the original integral in terms of simpler ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author demonstrates by taking differences relative to an index r (Av = 2 etc.), rewriting trig functions with shifted arguments, introducing k substitutions, and relating integrals of sin(rx)(sin a)^m to combinations involving simpler integrals and known sequences (A2n etc.). This method yields many concrete reduction formulae.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operator method: apply polynomial/differential operators to known integrals
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat functional expressions F(D) of the differentiation operator D acting on exponentials or trig functions (e^{-x}, sin(px), cos(px)) to generate identities that express parametrically-weighted integrals in terms of known base integrals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: (1−kD)^m e^{-x} expansions and relations such as ∫ e^{-x} f(x) dx = F(D)X where X is a basic integral. The paper lists formulas (23)–(30) showing how to get integrals like ∫ e^{-x} sin(px)(1−k x)^m dx from base X via operator actions; these may be differentiated further in parameters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional-equation approach to resultant of two equal forces (Poisson)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume resultant R of two equal forces P separated by angle 2θ has form R = P·Φ(θ). By decomposing one force into two equal components and equating resultants of grouped forces, obtain a functional equation for Φ(θ) which determines its form up to constants; determine constants from three known physical cases (θ = 0, θ = π/2, θ = 120°).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solve the resulting functional equation by trying exponential or trigonometric ansätze (Ae^{aθ} + A'e^{-aθ} or C cos(aθ) + C' sin(aθ)); apply boundary/physical conditions (same direction ⇒ R=2P; opposite ⇒ R=0; three at 120° ⇒ combined zero) to fix constants; reject spurious complex/infinite solutions on physical grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical synthesis by digit-by-digit (Horner-style) methods
rubrics_metrics.description: In numerical synthetical operations (e.g., computing integer powers), treat the digits of the root as increments ordered optionally (commonly from least significant digit), use a running multiplier, and apply successive partial multiplications and additions to build the final power (Horner-like procedure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by computing the cube of 835271: start with final digit, use coefficients corresponding to powers and accumulated partial products; the order of digits is optional but affects bookkeeping. This is Horner's practical algorithmic viewpoint for polynomial evaluation/synthesis.
